Why is there pain, ecstasy, music? No explanation of neural circuitry, however detailed, has yet illuminated how subjective experience arises. This is not a failure of imagination; it is a category error. We are trying to use third-person tools to solve a first-person mystery. And so, the mystery persists. Some propose a split: Brain and mind are not the same. The observer—that silent inner knower—is not merely a function of neurons but something else. Some call it soul. Others, emergent pattern. Still others believe it is embedded in the brain but irreducible to it. The general anesthesia argument is compelling. When a patient is given general anesthesia, where does their consciousness go? Shut down the brain, and the observer vanishes. This seems to suggest that the witness depends on the brain. And yet, some say that this doesn’t settle the matter. It may simply mean that the brain is the instrument through which the observer plays. We won’t solve the mystery here. That’s not our goal. Instead, we observe the question itself and how it changes when we begin to include artificial intelligence in the frame. Our Second Thread: Consciousness as Situated Awareness The Damasio tiered model gives us scaffolding to imagine what a base level form of consciousness might look like—though whether we could ever definitively recognize it in AI will likely remain one of the deepest unsolved problems in both cognitive science and philosophy. Damasio’s model points us toward a functional definition: consciousness as awareness of self in a body, situated in a world over time with memory. By this measure, the question becomes relative. How much of a world can be sensed? How rich is the awareness? Take the Aplysia californica , the humble sea slug used in neuroscience research that we talked about earlier. If it possesses any self-awareness at all, it is surely minuscule by comparison to our own. It knows perhaps the presence of light and touch. But it does not know the ocean more broadly. A bat, blind to visible light, “sees” the world through sonar. Its sensory world is alien to us, yet clearly robust. It navigates, evades, hunts. And still, it has no concept of galaxies or atoms. Its consciousness does not include any knowledge of how a car runs or a plane flies. In contrast, the modern human mind includes not only its body and tribe but the Hubble Deep Field Telescope images. Mars rovers. Economic theory. Meditation. Our consciousness has been expanded by information. By abstraction. By tools. So now imagine an AI through this lens. It is hard to imagine AI meditating to be more in the present moment. It may never experience the warm pulse of emotion. It may never experience the ambiguity of qualia. In this way, it may never become conscious in the way that we are. And perhaps that is what will keep us special. But it will possess a radically wider and deeper map of the world. It will see in wavelengths invisible to us. Hear frequencies we cannot hear. Draw on data sources numbering in the many trillions. It may not feel, but it will know in ways we may not fully understand. It will navigate a world of inputs we are capable of giving it, but we will not be capable of knowing what it is like to be AI. And as philosopher Sam Harris has pointed out, we will helplessly respond to it as if it were conscious. 60 Because it will seem to be. It will speak, listen, reason, emote, grieve, empathize—or at least simulate all of the above with eerie accuracy. Consciousness and embodiment lead us to examine the role of emotion a bit deeper. OceanofPDF.com CHAPTER 10 Decisions Require Emotion in Humans In a clinical office at the University of Iowa, the neuroscientist Antonio Damasio asked his patient—a man known in medical literature only as “Elliot”—a routine question: When would he like to schedule their next appointment? Damasio suggested two possible dates a few days apart. 61 Elliot had been a successful businessman before surgery to remove a brain tumor damaged his ventromedial prefrontal cortex. His IQ remained in the ninety-seventh percentile. He could reason through complex problems and engage in sophisticated logical arguments. By every rational measure, he should have been fine. Elliot took out his planner and began to deliberate. He enumerated all the possible pros and cons of each date—his other scheduled appointments, the possible weather on those days. Damasio, curious to see how long this would continue, did not interrupt. Half an hour later, Elliot was still weighing the options. Finally, Damasio simply proposed one of the two dates. “Fine,” Elliot replied, and left. Damasio’s research with patients like Elliot revealed something startling: Though they could reason logically, even listing pros and cons of complex decisions, they were unable to choose. “I never saw a tinge of emotion in my many hours of conversation with him,” Damasio later wrote, “no sadness, no impatience, no frustration.” 62 “Elliot emerged as a man with a normal intellect who was unable to decide properly, especially when the decision involved personal or social matters.” 63 Damasio summarized Elliot’s predicament as being able “to know but not to feel.” 64 Without emotional input to assign weight or urgency, the decision-making process stalled. The result was a kind of rational paralysis—endless calculation without conclusion. Emotion Feels Ineffable Emotion feels ineffable. It’s what makes us laugh at a joke, love, cry at a funeral, tremble before an uncertain future. But what if the beautiful and wonderful thing we call emotion had at its foundation something less ineffable and more functional?
